lessons.title: Physical, Emotional and Social Wellbeing
lessons.description: How sport supports physical, mental and social health and reduces health risks.
lessons.content_html:
What Do We Mean by Health and Wellbeing?

When people talk about being healthy, they often think only about the body — whether someone is fit, slim or free from illness. But health is a much broader concept. The World Health Organization defines health as a state of complete physical, emotional and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. That means a person who is physically fit but socially isolated or constantly anxious is not fully healthy. Understanding all three dimensions of health is essential for explaining how sport and physical activity contribute to a person’s overall wellbeing.

Physical Health

Physical health relates to how well the body functions. Participation in regular physical activity improves physical health in several measurable ways. Cardiovascular fitness improves as the heart becomes stronger and more efficient, lowering resting heart rate and blood pressure. Muscular strength and endurance increase as muscle fibres are recruited and adapted through training. Flexibility improves as joints are taken through a greater range of motion. Body composition shifts as fat mass decreases and lean muscle mass increases. Together, these changes reduce the risk of a range of serious health conditions. Regular physical activity lowers the risk of coronary heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity and osteoporosis. A 35-year-old recreational swimmer who trains three times per week will typically have a lower resting blood pressure, a healthier body weight and stronger bones than a sedentary peer of the same age.

Key Fact

Regular physical activity improves cardiovascular fitness (reducing the risk of coronary heart disease), improves body composition (reducing obesity risk) and increases bone density (reducing the risk of osteoporosis). Each benefit is achieved through specific physiological adaptations during training.

Emotional Health

Emotional health (sometimes called psychological health) refers to a person’s ability to manage feelings and cope with the demands of daily life. Physical activity has a powerful positive effect on emotional wellbeing. Exercise triggers the release of endorphins — natural brain chemicals that create a sense of wellbeing. This is why people often describe a feeling of euphoria after an intense workout or run. Beyond the biochemical effect, regular physical activity has been shown to reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression. It provides a constructive outlet for stress, improves sleep quality and builds confidence as performers see their skills and fitness improve over time.

Sport also provides a sense of purpose, structure and achievement. A teenager who joins a football team has a reason to train, a community to belong to and goals to work towards. Meeting and exceeding personal targets — running a faster mile, scoring a first goal, learning a new gymnastic routine — builds self-esteem. Elite athletes such as Dame Kelly Holmes and Marcus Rashford have spoken publicly about how sport helped them manage mental health challenges, illustrating that the psychological benefits apply at every level of participation.

A common error is to focus only on physical benefits when answering questions about health and wellbeing. Mark schemes reward all three dimensions. For emotional health, a strong answer names the mechanism (endorphin release), the outcome (reduced anxiety/improved mood) and applies it to a realistic scenario. For example: “Taking part in a weekly yoga class reduces cortisol levels and promotes endorphin release, which has been shown to reduce symptoms of mild depression.” Naming the specific benefit and mechanism earns marks; vague phrases like “it makes you feel better” do not.

Social Health

Social health refers to a person’s ability to form and maintain relationships and function within society. Sport and physical activity are uniquely powerful tools for improving social health because they bring people together through shared goals. Team sports such as netball, rugby and basketball require communication, cooperation and mutual trust. Playing together regularly builds friendships, a sense of belonging and social identity. Players who train with the same club for several years often describe the team as a second family.

Beyond team sports, even individual activities carried out in a group context — a running club, a gym class, a swimming squad — provide social contact. This is particularly important for people who are at risk of social isolation, such as older adults or those recovering from injury. Community sport programmes have been used as a public health tool to reduce loneliness and build social cohesion in areas where community bonds have weakened.

Key Fact

Social health benefits of sport include: developing communication and cooperation skills (team sports), building friendships and a sense of belonging (club membership), and reducing social isolation (community sport programmes). Social health improves when sport connects people, not just when it is played.

Positive and Negative Effects of Fitness on Wellbeing

While the benefits of physical activity are well established, it is important to recognise that there can also be negative effects when activity levels are excessive or poorly managed. Overtraining can lead to physical exhaustion, increased injury risk, and — at its most extreme — burnout. Compulsive exercising, sometimes called exercise addiction, can become psychologically harmful if a person feels unable to rest without guilt or anxiety. Pressure to achieve a particular body image through sport can contribute to disordered eating, particularly in sports where weight or aesthetic appearance is judged, such as gymnastics, rowing or wrestling. These negative effects highlight the importance of balance: physical activity should promote wellbeing, not replace one set of health risks with another.

A useful exam technique for 9-mark evaluate questions is to apply all three health dimensions to the same scenario. For example, a 50-year-old who joins a local park run group would gain: physical benefits (improved cardiovascular fitness, reduced blood pressure, healthier weight); emotional benefits (stress relief through endorphin release, improved confidence as times improve); and social benefits (new friendships, sense of community, reduced isolation). A top-band answer evaluates whether these benefits outweigh any risks (overuse injury, time commitment) and reaches a clear, justified conclusion.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain’ questions about health benefits, use the three-step structure: name the benefit, explain the mechanism (how exercise achieves it), and apply it to a sporting example. A common mistake is to confuse physical, emotional and social health — remember: physical = body functions; emotional = feelings and mental state; social = relationships and interaction. For 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ questions on wellbeing, always include both positive and negative effects, apply each to a sport or athlete, and reach a conclusion that weighs up the balance. One-sided answers that only describe benefits will not reach the top band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health has three dimensions: physical (body function, fitness, disease prevention), emotional (mood, mental wellbeing, stress management) and social (relationships, belonging, community). Sport can improve all three simultaneously.
  • Physical activity reduces health risks including coronary heart disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes and osteoporosis. Endorphin release during exercise underpins many emotional benefits, including reduced anxiety and improved mood.
  • Negative effects are possible with excess or unhealthy engagement — overtraining, exercise addiction and disordered eating can undermine the very health benefits that sport is meant to promote. Balance is essential.

Which of the following best describes emotional health?
A) The absence of physical injury
B) The ability to manage feelings and respond to stress constructively
C) The ability to perform sport at a high level

practice_questions.text: Identify one physical health benefit and one social health benefit of regular participation in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any physical health benefit, correctly identified (e.g. improved cardiovascular fitness / reduced risk of coronary heart disease / improved body composition / reduced risk of obesity / increased bone density). 1 mark for any social health benefit, correctly identified (e.g. improved communication and cooperation skills / making friends / reduced social isolation / sense of belonging through team membership).

practice_questions.text: Explain how regular participation in sport can improve a person's emotional health.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for naming the mechanism (e.g. exercise triggers endorphin release); 1 mark for explaining the outcome (e.g. endorphins reduce anxiety and improve mood / create a sense of wellbeing); 1 mark for applying to a realistic sporting context (e.g. a swimmer who trains three times per week reports lower stress levels and better sleep quality as a result of the endorphin response during training).

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old joins a local athletics club after a period of low mood and social isolation. Explain how club membership could improve two different dimensions of her health.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for correctly identifying two different health dimensions (e.g. emotional + social). 1 mark each for explaining how the club addresses each dimension. Acceptable content: emotional — structured training goals and achievement of personal bests builds confidence and self-esteem; training triggers endorphin release reducing anxiety; social — training with peers builds friendships and a sense of belonging; shared goals in the team create cooperative bonds that reduce isolation.

practice_questions.text: A club-level cyclist has increased her training volume significantly over the past three months. Analyse the potential positive and negative effects of this increased training on her health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Positive and negative effects discussed across at least two health dimensions; each effect is linked to a specific mechanism (e.g. endorphin release for emotional benefit; overtraining causing fatigue/immune suppression as a negative); consistent application to the cycling context; technically accurate language throughout.

Secure: Both positive and negative effects present; at least two health dimensions touched on; mostly accurate; cycling application present but may be general.

Developing: Either positive or negative effects discussed more fully; limited to one health dimension; some sporting application.

Emerging: Basic list of benefits or risks with little development or sporting application.

Acceptable positive content: improved cardiovascular fitness (reduced coronary heart disease risk); improved body composition; endorphin release improving mood; increased self-confidence as performance improves; social bonds with training partners.
Acceptable negative content: overtraining leading to physical exhaustion, increased injury risk; compulsive training can cause anxiety if rest feels impossible; pressure around body weight/composition in cycling can contribute to disordered eating; social withdrawal if training takes priority over other relationships.

practice_questions.text: A young athlete claims: ‘Sport is always good for your health — there are no downsides.’ Evaluate this statement, considering all three dimensions of health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full discussion across all three health dimensions (physical, emotional, social); balanced argument covering both benefits and risks; consistent sporting application; clear justified conclusion that challenges the athlete’s claim while recognising the genuine benefits.

Secure: At least two dimensions discussed; both benefits and risks present; some sporting application; conclusion present.

Developing: Mainly benefits discussed; limited to one or two dimensions; limited sporting application; argument largely one-sided.

Emerging: Basic list of health benefits with little or no discussion of risks or dimensions.

Agreeing (sport is good): physical benefits (cardiovascular fitness, reduced obesity/CHD/diabetes risk); emotional benefits (endorphin release, reduced anxiety, improved self-esteem); social benefits (teamwork, friendships, community belonging).

Disagreeing / partial challenge: overtraining can cause physical injury, fatigue and immune suppression; exercise addiction can increase anxiety rather than reduce it; social pressure in sport can lead to unhealthy body-image concerns and disordered eating; elite sport demands can isolate athletes from non-sporting social relationships.

Conclusion: Sport is broadly beneficial across all three health dimensions, but the benefits are maximised when training is balanced, goals are healthy, and participation is enjoyable rather than compulsive.

lessons.title: Lifestyle Choices and Sedentary Living
lessons.description: Diet, sleep, alcohol, smoking and the long-term health risks of a sedentary lifestyle.
lessons.content_html:
Lifestyle and Its Impact on Health

The choices a person makes every day — what they eat, how much they move, how they sleep, whether they use recreational drugs — accumulate over time to shape their long-term health. These are known as lifestyle choices. Understanding which choices promote health and which ones damage it is fundamental to physical education because it connects the theory of the body to the reality of how people live. The spec identifies four key lifestyle factors: diet, activity level, work/rest/sleep balance, and the use of recreational drugs (alcohol and nicotine).

Diet

A balanced diet provides the energy and nutrients the body needs to function well. The key macronutrient proportions for a healthy, active individual are approximately 55–60% carbohydrates, 25–30% fats and 15–20% protein. Carbohydrates are the primary fuel for physical activity, particularly moderate-to-high-intensity exercise. Protein is essential for muscle repair and growth after training. Fats support hormone production, cell function and provide fuel for low-intensity, prolonged exercise. Vitamins and minerals (micronutrients) are needed in smaller amounts but support vital functions such as immune defence, oxygen transport (iron) and bone formation (calcium and vitamin D).

Poor diet choices can have serious long-term consequences. A diet consistently high in saturated fat and refined sugar raises low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, contributing to atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease. A high-calorie, low-nutrient diet causes weight gain and, if sustained, leads to obesity. A diet lacking in calcium and vitamin D weakens bones, increasing the risk of osteoporosis. Insufficient iron intake can cause anaemia, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood and impairing exercise performance.

Work/Rest/Sleep Balance

The body does not adapt to training during exercise — it adapts during rest and recovery. Insufficient sleep disrupts the release of growth hormone, which is essential for muscle repair. Chronically poor sleep is associated with weight gain (due to disrupted appetite hormones), increased injury risk and reduced concentration, which impairs the decision-making needed in sport. For athletes, 8–9 hours of sleep per night is generally recommended, though individual needs vary. An imbalanced lifestyle where work or social pressures chronically reduce sleep time can negate the benefits of regular training.

Key Fact

The four lifestyle factors are: diet (balanced nutrition vs poor food choices), activity level (regular exercise vs sedentary behaviour), work/rest/sleep balance (adequate recovery vs chronic sleep deprivation), and use of recreational drugs (abstaining vs smoking or alcohol use). Each factor can either protect health or increase risk of disease.

Recreational Drugs: Alcohol and Nicotine

Nicotine is the addictive substance in tobacco. Smoking damages the respiratory system progressively. The tar in cigarette smoke coats the alveoli, reducing the surface area available for gas exchange and lowering the efficiency of oxygen delivery to muscles. Carbon monoxide in smoke binds to haemoglobin in place of oxygen, further reducing the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity. Long-term consequences of smoking include bronchitis (inflammation of the bronchi, causing persistent cough and breathlessness), emphysema (destruction of alveoli, causing severe breathlessness) and lung cancer. Smokers have significantly reduced cardiovascular endurance and are less able to sustain aerobic activity. A 16-year-old who smokes regularly will have measurably worse performance on a Cooper 12-minute run test than a non-smoking peer of the same training background.

Alcohol is a depressant drug that slows the central nervous system. Short-term effects relevant to sport include impaired reaction time, reduced coordination and decreased balance — all of which reduce performance and increase injury risk. Long-term excessive alcohol consumption damages the liver (cirrhosis), raises blood pressure, contributes to weight gain (alcohol is high in calories with no nutritional value) and weakens the immune system. Alcohol also disrupts sleep quality, compounding the recovery problems described above. Athletes who regularly consume alcohol in large quantities find that their cardiovascular fitness, strength adaptations and recovery rates all deteriorate over time.

Carbon monoxide from cigarette smoke binds to haemoglobin with an affinity 200 times greater than oxygen. This means a smoker’s haemoglobin is partially ‘blocked’ and cannot carry as much oxygen to working muscles. The result is that cardiac output must increase to compensate, raising heart rate for the same submaximal workload. The smoker’s maximum aerobic capacity (VO2 max) is measurably lower. Additionally, nicotine causes vasoconstriction — narrowing of blood vessels — which raises blood pressure and reduces blood flow to the working muscles. On a mark scheme, naming the mechanism (carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin; tar coats alveoli) earns more marks than simply stating “smoking reduces fitness.”

Sedentary Lifestyle and Its Consequences

A sedentary lifestyle is one that involves little or no regular physical activity. As a result of reduced energy expenditure, the body stores excess energy as fat, leading to being overweight or, in more serious cases, clinically obese. The consequences extend far beyond body weight. Without regular exercise, the cardiovascular system deteriorates: resting heart rate rises, blood pressure increases and the risk of coronary heart disease escalates significantly.

Sedentary individuals have lower insulin sensitivity, increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes. Inactivity weakens muscles through atrophy and reduces bone density, elevating the risk of osteoporosis. Posture deteriorates as postural muscles weaken from disuse, contributing to chronic back pain. Mental health is also affected: sedentary people have higher rates of depression and anxiety, partly because they miss the endorphin benefits of exercise and partly because sedentary activities (such as excessive screen time) displace social interaction and purposeful activity.

Students sometimes use these three terms interchangeably, but they have distinct meanings. Overweight refers to body mass above what is considered healthy for a person’s height (typically BMI > 25). Overfat refers specifically to excess body fat regardless of total weight — a heavily muscled athlete might be overweight by BMI but not overfat. Obese is a clinical classification (BMI > 30) associated with serious long-term health risks. The spec uses all three terms and a mark scheme will reward the correct term for the context described.

Key Fact

Consequences of a sedentary lifestyle include: overweight/obesity, coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, loss of muscle tone and poor posture, and depression/anxiety. These span all three dimensions of health and are all reducible through regular physical activity.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about smoking and health, always name the specific mechanism rather than saying “it reduces fitness.” For example: “Carbon monoxide from tobacco smoke binds to haemoglobin, reducing the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity.” That earns the mark — vague statements do not. For sedentary lifestyle questions, list consequences across different body systems (cardiovascular, skeletal, muscular, psychological) to demonstrate breadth. A common mistake is to list only physical consequences such as obesity; mark schemes also reward depression and anxiety as effects of inactivity. When using the terms overweight, overfat and obese, use them precisely — they are not synonyms.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four key lifestyle factors are diet, activity level, work/rest/sleep balance and use of recreational drugs. Positive choices in each area protect health; negative choices increase risk of long-term disease.
  • Smoking reduces oxygen delivery to muscles via carbon monoxide binding to haemoglobin and tar coating the alveoli; long-term consequences include bronchitis, emphysema and lung cancer. Alcohol impairs reaction time, coordination and sleep quality.
  • A sedentary lifestyle leads to obesity, coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, muscle loss and depression — consequences spanning all three dimensions of health.

practice_questions.text: State one long-term consequence of a sedentary lifestyle on cardiovascular health.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid cardiovascular consequence: increased risk of coronary heart disease / raised blood pressure / increased resting heart rate / increased risk of type 2 diabetes (credit as cardiovascular consequence via insulin resistance link).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'sedentary lifestyle'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying lack of physical activity as the key feature (e.g. little or no regular exercise / predominantly inactive behaviour); 1 mark for contextualising with an example or the health consequence (e.g. typically involves prolonged sitting, screen time or desk-based work, leading to low energy expenditure and accumulation of excess body fat).

practice_questions.text: Describe how smoking reduces a performer's ability to sustain aerobic exercise.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that carbon monoxide in smoke binds to haemoglobin, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity; 1 mark for explaining that tar coats the alveoli, reducing the surface area for gas exchange and lowering the efficiency of oxygen absorption; 1 mark for stating the consequence for performance (the working muscles receive less oxygen, so the performer fatigues more quickly during sustained aerobic activity such as distance running).

practice_questions.text: Table 1 shows the average weekly hours of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity for two groups of 16-year-old students. Group A: 5.8 hours. Group B: 0.9 hours. Interpret what this data suggests about the likely long-term health outcomes for students in Group B.

practice_questions.text: A secondary school introduces a daily 20-minute active break for all students in response to concerns about sedentary behaviour. Assess whether this intervention is likely to improve students' health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Factors supporting and questioning the intervention are weighed; health benefits explained with mechanisms (e.g. daily moderate activity raises heart rate, improves cardiovascular fitness, reduces obesity risk, triggers endorphin release improving mood); limitations acknowledged (e.g. 20 minutes may be insufficient; intensity matters; benefits depend on whether students are sedentary outside school); reasoned judgement reached.

Secure: Benefits and limitations both present; mostly accurate physiological explanation; reasoned conclusion.

Developing: Mainly benefits described; limited physiological mechanism; little evaluation of whether the intervention is sufficient.

Emerging: Basic statement that exercise is good with little development.

Acceptable content in support: daily activity raises heart rate and improves cardiovascular fitness over time; endorphin release improves emotional wellbeing; structured movement reduces prolonged sitting; social interaction during the break improves social health. Limitations: 20 minutes is relatively short; benefit depends on intensity; students may still be sedentary for the other 23+ hours; the intervention does not address diet or sleep.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which lifestyle choices are the most important factor in determining a person's long-term health outcomes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation across multiple lifestyle factors (diet, activity, sleep, alcohol/smoking); consideration of other determinants of health (genetics, socio-economic status, healthcare access); consistent sporting or health examples; justified conclusion that acknowledges lifestyle as highly important while recognising it is not the sole determinant.

Secure: At least three lifestyle factors covered; some acknowledgement of other health determinants; sporting examples present; conclusion reached.

Developing: Mainly lifestyle factors described with limited evaluation; other health determinants absent or minimal; argument largely one-sided.

Emerging: Basic list of lifestyle factors with no evaluative structure.

Agreeing (lifestyle is most important): diet, activity level, sleep and avoidance of alcohol/smoking account for the largest share of preventable disease; regular exercise reduces risk of CHD, obesity, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis; smoking causes bronchitis/lung cancer; diet drives body composition.

Partial challenge: genetics influence susceptibility to disease regardless of lifestyle (e.g. familial hypercholesterolaemia); socio-economic factors limit access to healthy food and safe exercise spaces; access to healthcare affects early detection and treatment of disease. Conclusion: lifestyle choices are the single most modifiable and impactful factor for most people, but they interact with non-modifiable factors such as genetics and structural inequalities.

lessons.title: Diet, Nutrition and Hydration
lessons.description: Macronutrients, micronutrients, energy balance and how dehydration affects sport performance.
lessons.content_html:
Why Nutrition Matters in Sport

Food is the body’s fuel. The amount, type and timing of what an athlete eats directly affects how much energy they have during training, how quickly they recover afterwards, whether their body composition supports their sport and how strongly their immune and skeletal systems resist injury and illness. A thorough understanding of nutrition is therefore not a separate subject from PE — it is integral to physical performance.

Macronutrients

Macronutrients are the energy-providing nutrients. The three macronutrients are carbohydrates, fats and proteins. A balanced diet for an active individual should provide approximately 55–60% of energy from carbohydrates, 25–30% from fats and 15–20% from proteins.

Carbohydrates are the body’s preferred and most readily available energy source. They are broken down to glucose, which is used directly for energy production or stored as glycogen in the liver and skeletal muscles. Glycogen is the key fuel for moderate-to-high-intensity exercise. When glycogen stores are depleted, performance deteriorates rapidly — athletes call this “hitting the wall” in endurance events. Carbohydrate loading is a strategy used by endurance athletes such as marathon runners, who increase carbohydrate intake in the days before a race to maximise glycogen stores. A runner preparing for a marathon might shift from a standard 55% carbohydrate diet to 70% in the final 48 hours before the race.

Proteins are made up of amino acids and are essential for the growth, repair and maintenance of body tissues, particularly muscle. During resistance training, microscopic tears occur in muscle fibres. Protein consumed after training provides the amino acids needed to repair these tears and build new, stronger muscle tissue — a process called hypertrophy. The timing of protein intake matters: consuming protein within 30–60 minutes after a resistance session maximises the muscle-repair response. For power athletes such as weightlifters or sprinters, protein intake is especially important because muscle mass is central to their performance.

Fats are a concentrated energy source providing more than twice the energy per gram as carbohydrates or proteins. They are the primary fuel for low-intensity, prolonged exercise — long, easy-paced cycling or walking. The body stores fat in virtually unlimited quantities and draws on it during aerobic activity when glycogen stores begin to deplete. Fats are also essential for the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), the production of hormones and the maintenance of cell membranes. Unsaturated fats from sources such as olive oil, nuts and oily fish are health-promoting, whereas excessive saturated fat (from red meat and full-fat dairy) raises LDL cholesterol and increases cardiovascular disease risk.

Key Fact

Balanced diet macronutrient split: carbohydrates 55–60% (primary fuel, stored as glycogen), fats 25–30% (secondary fuel, hormone production), proteins 15–20% (tissue repair and hypertrophy). Endurance athletes increase carbohydrate proportion before major events; power athletes prioritise protein timing after resistance training.

Micronutrients

Micronutrients — vitamins and minerals — do not provide energy but are essential for many critical processes. Iron is needed to form haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells; a deficiency causes anaemia, reducing aerobic capacity. Calcium is the primary mineral in bone structure; adequate calcium intake throughout adolescence maximises bone density, reducing lifelong fracture risk. Vitamin D enables calcium absorption from the gut and is therefore equally important for bone health. Athletes who train indoors or in low-sunlight climates may develop vitamin D deficiency, increasing their risk of stress fractures. Water and fibre, while not traditional micronutrients, are also essential: fibre supports healthy digestion and water enables every cellular process in the body.

Many students believe that eating large amounts of protein will automatically cause muscle bulk. In reality, dietary protein alone does not cause hypertrophy — it must be combined with progressive resistance training. Protein provides the raw material (amino acids) for muscle repair; the training stimulus provides the reason to repair bigger. An endurance athlete who increases protein intake without changing their training will simply excrete the excess as urea rather than building new muscle. This is an important nuance for 4-mark explain questions about nutrition and performance.

Energy Balance

Energy balance is the relationship between energy consumed (through food and drink) and energy expended (through basal metabolic rate and physical activity). When intake equals expenditure, weight is stable. When intake exceeds expenditure, the surplus is stored as fat and weight increases. When expenditure exceeds intake, the body draws on fat stores and weight decreases. Maintaining an appropriate energy balance is essential for athletes: too little energy causes fatigue, muscle loss and hormonal disruption; too much causes unwanted fat gain and reduced power-to-weight ratio. The correct balance varies between sports: an ultra-endurance athlete needs a very high caloric intake, while a gymnast needs carefully controlled intake to maintain the strength-to-weight ratio that their sport demands.

Hydration and Dehydration

Water makes up around 60% of adult body mass and is involved in every physiological process relevant to exercise: transporting nutrients and oxygen in the blood, regulating body temperature through sweating, lubricating joints and removing waste products via urine. Even mild dehydration — a loss of just 2% of body water — measurably impairs aerobic performance and decision-making ability. As dehydration worsens, blood volume decreases, which makes the blood thicker. This raises blood viscosity, forcing the heart to work harder to deliver the same amount of oxygen to the muscles. Heart rate rises, perceived effort increases and endurance performance deteriorates.

At higher levels of dehydration (above 5% body water loss), the risk of heat exhaustion and heat stroke increases significantly. Cramping, dizziness and collapse become possible during prolonged exercise in warm conditions. Athletes should begin exercise well hydrated (pale yellow urine is a common guide) and drink regularly throughout prolonged activity rather than waiting until they feel thirsty — thirst is already a late signal of dehydration. Sports drinks that contain electrolytes (sodium and potassium) as well as carbohydrates are useful in events lasting more than 60 minutes, as they replace both fluid and the electrolytes lost in sweat.

Key Fact

Dehydration chain: blood volume decreases → blood viscosity increases → heart works harder to maintain cardiac output → heart rate rises → fatigue increases and endurance performance deteriorates. Even 2% dehydration measurably impairs aerobic performance.

Carbohydrate loading works by maximising glycogen storage in the muscles and liver before a prolonged endurance event. Athletes typically taper their training (reducing volume while maintaining intensity) and simultaneously increase carbohydrate intake in the 48–72 hours before competition. The strategy is effective for events lasting more than 90 minutes (such as a marathon or triathlon) because it delays the point at which glycogen depletion causes fatigue. It is not appropriate for short, high-intensity events (such as the 100m sprint) where glycogen stores are not the limiting factor. A sprinter does not benefit from carbohydrate loading in the same way because their event is over in under 15 seconds and relies primarily on the ATP-PC (phosphocreatine) energy system.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about macronutrients, always name the specific function of each one, not just “they provide energy.” Carbohydrates for fuel and glycogen storage; protein for muscle repair and hypertrophy; fats for low-intensity fuel and hormone production — these distinctions earn the marks. For dehydration questions, describe the physiological chain of events (blood volume → viscosity → heart rate) rather than simply saying “you get tired.” A common mistake on calculate questions involving energy balance or macronutrient percentages is to forget to show the calculation — always write the formula, substitute the values and state the unit in your answer.

Key Takeaways

  • Macronutrient split for an active person: 55–60% carbohydrates (primary fuel, glycogen), 25–30% fats (secondary fuel, hormones), 15–20% protein (repair and hypertrophy). Timing matters: protein within 60 minutes post-resistance training maximises adaptation.
  • Micronutrients such as iron (haemoglobin, aerobic capacity) and calcium (bone density) are essential for performance. Deficiency in either can directly impair training outcomes or increase injury risk.
  • Dehydration reduces blood volume, increases blood viscosity, raises heart rate and reduces endurance performance — even 2% water loss is measurable. Athletes should maintain hydration before, during and after exercise.

In favour: maximises muscle and liver glycogen stores; delays the point of glycogen depletion ('hitting the wall') in events over 90 minutes; allows the athlete to maintain race pace for longer; particularly effective for marathon runners, cyclists and triathletes who perform for 2+ hours.

lessons.title: Classification of Skills and Practice Structures
lessons.description: Basic/complex, open/closed and high/low organisation continua, and matching practice to skill type.
lessons.content_html:
Why Classify Skills?

Not all sporting skills are the same. A tennis serve differs fundamentally from a football tackle, which differs again from a gymnastics routine. Understanding what makes skills different — and what those differences mean for how they should be taught and practised — is at the heart of sport psychology in this unit. The spec organises skills along three distinct continua, each describing a different characteristic. These continua are not the same as each other and skills can sit at different positions on different continua simultaneously.

Continuum 1: Basic to Complex

The basic-to-complex continuum describes the cognitive and movement demands of a skill. A basic skill involves few decisions, requires little information processing and can be learned quickly. Running in a straight line, catching a stationary ball or performing a single squat are basic skills. A complex skill involves many simultaneous decisions, high information processing demands and often requires coordination of multiple body segments. A gymnastic floor routine, a cricket batting stroke under pressure or a basketball lay-up involve complex decision-making and precise sequencing. Complex skills take much longer to learn and require more structured, progressive practice.

Continuum 2: Open to Closed

The open-to-closed continuum describes whether the environment in which a skill is performed is stable or unpredictable. An open skill is performed in a changing environment where the performer must constantly read and react to external cues. Tackling in rugby, receiving a serve in badminton and dribbling past a defender in basketball are all open skills — the environment (opponents, teammates, ball trajectory) changes unpredictably from moment to moment. A closed skill is performed in a stable, predictable environment where the performer controls the pace and conditions. A gymnastics vault, a darts throw or a golf drive from the tee are closed skills — there is no opponent to react to and the environment does not change.

One of the most common errors in sport psychology questions is to confuse the three continua. They are separate dimensions. A skill can be open AND complex (football dribbling under pressure), open AND basic (a beginner's walking stride in a crowd), closed AND complex (a gymnastic floor routine) or closed AND basic (a stationary press-up). Similarly, high organisation does not mean complex. Always apply each continuum independently and explain which feature of the skill determines its position on each one. Mark schemes award a mark for each continuum correctly applied — mixing them up costs marks.

Continuum 3: High to Low Organisation

The high-to-low organisation continuum describes the degree to which a skill’s subroutines (component parts) are interdependent. A high-organisation skill is one where the subroutines are so tightly linked that separating them destroys the skill. A golf swing, a javelin throw or a gymnastics tumbling pass are high-organisation skills — the backswing, the drive and the follow-through must flow seamlessly; practising them in isolation produces a disjointed, ineffective movement. A low-organisation skill can be broken down into its component parts and each part practised separately without destroying the integrity of the whole. Swimming the front crawl has relatively low organisation: the arm pull, the kick and the breathing can each be practised in isolation using floats or fins, then recombined. This distinction is crucial because it determines whether whole practice or part practice is more appropriate.

Key Fact

Three continua: (1) Basic (few decisions, quick to learn, e.g. a throw-in) to Complex (many decisions, slow to master, e.g. a triple jump); (2) Open (changing environment, e.g. a rugby tackle) to Closed (stable environment, e.g. a vault); (3) Low organisation (subroutines separable, e.g. front crawl) to High organisation (subroutines inseparable, e.g. a golf swing). A skill can sit at different points on each continuum independently.

Practice Structures

The classification of a skill should directly influence how it is practised. Four practice structures are required for this unit: massed, distributed, fixed and variable.

Massed practice involves practising the skill continuously with little or no rest. It is appropriate for simple, closed skills that need to become automatic through sheer repetition — for example, a beginner repeatedly practising a forward roll. The advantage is efficiency: a large amount of practice is compressed into a short time. The disadvantage is that fatigue sets in, which can cause technical errors to become ingrained and can demotivate performers, particularly learners.

Distributed practice breaks practice into shorter sessions separated by rest or other activities. It is better suited to complex skills or to learners who tire quickly. The rest intervals allow physical and mental recovery, reducing the risk of fatigue-induced errors and maintaining motivation. A coach who gives a beginner gymnast several short practice blocks with feedback and rest between them is using distributed practice.

Fixed practice (also called blocked practice) involves rehearsing a skill repeatedly under the same conditions without variation. It is ideal for closed skills — practising a penalty kick from the spot each time, or rehearsing a gymnastics vault on the same apparatus at the same height. The constancy of the environment allows the motor programme for the skill to become deeply automated. The disadvantage is that the skill may not transfer well to variable match conditions if it is only ever practised in a fixed setting.

Variable practice involves rehearsing the same skill across a variety of different conditions or contexts. It is most appropriate for open skills that will be performed in changing environments. A football coach who has players practise passing against one defender, then two, then in small-sided games is using variable practice. The advantage is that performers develop the ability to adapt their execution to different environmental demands — which is what match play requires. The disadvantage is that the skill may not reach the same level of automation as quickly as with fixed practice.

Key Fact

Matching practice to skill: closed skills suit fixed practice (golf swing, gymnastics vault); open skills suit variable practice (football passing, rugby tackle); complex skills benefit from distributed practice to prevent fatigue errors; simple skills can use massed practice to build automaticity quickly. Using the wrong practice type can embed errors or fail to prepare the performer for match conditions.

The high/low organisation continuum directly determines whether whole or part practice should be used. High-organisation skills such as the golf swing or a free throw in basketball should be practised as a whole, because breaking them into parts disrupts the timing and sequencing that make them effective. Low-organisation skills such as swimming strokes or a tennis serve can be broken into parts — practising the ball toss separately, the racket motion separately, then combining them — without losing the essence of the skill. A coach who tries to break a high-organisation skill into parts may inadvertently teach the performer to pause or fragment their movement, which is harder to correct later than if whole practice had been used from the start.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For classification questions, always explain which feature of the skill determines its position on the continuum — do not just label the skill. For example, “A tennis serve is a closed skill because the performer controls the timing and the environment does not change unpredictably during execution.” On practice structure questions, justify the choice by linking the practice type to the characteristic of the skill: “Variable practice is appropriate for an open skill like a rugby tackle because the performer needs to adapt their technique to changing conditions in a match.” The most common mark-scheme error is to confuse the three continua with each other — treat each as a separate question and apply one at a time.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Three separate continua: basic-complex (cognitive demand), open-closed (environmental stability), low-high organisation (separability of subroutines). A skill can sit at different points on all three independently — never conflate them.
  • Four practice structures: massed (continuous, suits simple closed skills), distributed (rest intervals, suits complex skills or learners), fixed (same conditions repeated, suits closed skills), variable (different conditions, suits open skills).
  • High-organisation skills should be practised whole; low-organisation skills can be broken into parts. Matching practice type to skill classification is the key principle a coach applies when designing sessions.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of massed practice for developing sporting skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of massed practice with specific examples of when it is effective and when it is harmful; skill type (basic vs complex, closed vs open) used to justify when massed practice is/isn't appropriate; fatigue, motivation and error-embedding discussed; balanced conclusion.

Secure: Both advantages and disadvantages present; some skill-type contextualisation; examples used; conclusion present.

Developing: Either advantages or disadvantages more fully developed; limited skill-type contextualisation; argument mainly descriptive.

Emerging: Basic description of massed practice with little evaluation.

Advantages: efficient use of time; builds automaticity quickly through high repetition volume; well-suited to basic, closed skills that need to become habitual (e.g. a basketball free-throw, a gymnastic arabesque); mentally motivating for performers who want to feel they are doing lots of training.

Disadvantages: fatigue causes breakdown in technique, which risks embedding errors that are hard to correct; demotivating for learners or younger performers; not suited to complex or open skills where quality of practice matters more than quantity; performer may lose focus during extended repetition, reducing the cognitive engagement needed to truly learn the skill. Conclusion: massed practice is valuable in limited contexts (basic, closed skills, experienced performers who can maintain quality while fatigued) but is generally less effective than distributed practice for learning complex or open skills at GCSE level.

lessons.title: Goal Setting and SMART Targets
lessons.description: How goal setting motivates performers and the SMART principles for writing effective sporting targets.
lessons.content_html:
Why Goal Setting Matters in Sport

Every elite athlete trains with purpose. A sprint hurdler does not simply run to “get faster” — she trains to beat her personal best by 0.3 seconds before the national championships in eight weeks. That specificity matters. Goal setting is the deliberate process of identifying and committing to specific targets that direct effort, maintain motivation and provide a measurable framework for progress. Without clear goals, training lacks direction, motivation fluctuates and it becomes impossible to judge whether performance is actually improving.

Goals operate at different time scales. Long-term goals describe a broad aspiration over months or years — qualifying for the county squad, completing a triathlon or earning a county colours award. Short-term goals are smaller, more immediate milestones — completing five training sessions this week, improving 30m sprint time by 0.1 seconds this month. Short-term goals provide the stepping stones that make long-term goals feel achievable. A performer who has only long-term goals without short-term checkpoints will often lose motivation because progress feels distant and abstract. The two types of goal work together: short-term goals build confidence, and that confidence sustains effort toward the long-term vision.

The SMART Framework

A goal is only as effective as its design. Vague goals like “get better at basketball” do not tell the performer what to do, how much progress is enough or when to review. The SMART framework provides five criteria that, when applied together, transform a vague aspiration into a precise, workable target.

Specific — the goal names the precise skill, activity or outcome being targeted. “Improve my basketball free throw” is more specific than “get better at basketball.” Being specific focuses training on exactly what needs to improve.

Measurable — the goal includes a number, percentage or observable criterion so that both the performer and the coach can judge whether it has been achieved. “Increase my free throw percentage from 40% to 60%” is measurable; “improve my free throw” is not. Without a measurable criterion, a goal cannot be evaluated.

Achievable — the goal is within the performer’s capability given their current level of fitness, skill and resources. An achievable goal challenges the performer without being so demanding that it is demoralising. A 16-year-old who can currently bench press 40 kg setting a goal to bench press 60 kg in eight weeks is probably not achievable and may lead to overtraining and injury. Raising it to 50 kg in eight weeks with a structured progression is more achievable.

Key Fact

SMART: Specific (names the exact skill/outcome), Measurable (includes a number or observable criterion), Achievable (within the performer’s current capability), Realistic (relevant to their sport and situation), Time-bound (has a deadline). Edexcel uses “Achievable” for the A — not “Accepted” or “Agreed.”

Realistic — the goal is relevant and appropriate to the performer’s sport, training context and current performance level. A footballer who wants to improve heading ability should set a realistic goal related to heading practice and match conditions, not one that requires expensive specialist equipment unavailable to them. Realistic is closely related to achievable but specifically addresses whether the goal fits the performer’s circumstances and context.

Time-bound — the goal has a clear deadline or review date. “By the end of the six-week training block” or “before the half-term fixture” creates urgency and provides a point at which progress can be formally assessed. Without a time boundary, goals drift indefinitely and the performer has no reason to work systematically. A time-bound goal also enables the performer to plan their training backwards from the deadline, ensuring enough time for progressive improvement.

Applying SMART in Practice

A poorly written goal: “I want to run faster.” A SMART goal: “I will reduce my 400m personal best from 64 seconds to 60 seconds by the end of the 8-week track season, by completing two speed-endurance sessions and one interval session per week.”

Breaking this down: it is specific (400m time), measurable (64 to 60 seconds), achievable (a 4-second improvement over 8 weeks is reasonable for a dedicated club athlete), realistic (relevant to the track season and the athlete’s training context) and time-bound (end of the 8-week season). Notice that the training method is also specified — this connects the goal to the process of achievement, which helps the performer understand what daily effort is required.

The most common error students make is writing targets that fail the Measurable or Time-bound criteria. A goal that says “I want to become a better swimmer” fails both. It also fails Specific. Another common mistake is writing a goal that is Specific but not Achievable — for example, “I will increase my vertical jump by 25 cm in one week.” Mark schemes for SMART target questions credit each criterion independently. If a question asks you to write a SMART target, check every letter: name the skill, include a number, make it genuinely challenging but achievable, keep it relevant to the performer and always include a deadline.

Goal Setting and Performance Enhancement

The psychological benefit of well-structured goal setting extends beyond simple direction. Goals that are accepted by the performer (rather than imposed by a coach) generate greater intrinsic motivation because the performer feels ownership of the target. Regularly reviewing and updating goals — raising targets when they are achieved, modifying them when injury or illness intervenes — keeps the goal framework current and relevant. Many elite coaches use goal setting as part of a formal pre-season planning process, with goals recorded and reviewed at fixed points. Intrinsic motivation is most strongly supported by goals that the performer believes are challenging but achievable — too easy and there is no sense of accomplishment; too hard and motivation collapses under repeated failure.

A useful distinction beyond the spec — useful for top-band answers — is between performance goals (targets about personal performance standards, e.g. run 10km in under 50 minutes) and outcome goals (targets about results or ranking, e.g. win the league). Performance goals are generally more powerful motivators because the performer has full control over them. Outcome goals depend partly on the quality of the opposition — a runner might achieve a lifetime best and still finish last in a strong field. Edexcel mark schemes reward application to specific sporting scenarios, so distinguishing performance from outcome goals in a 9-mark answer on motivation would place the response in the top band.

Key Fact

Effective goal setting improves performance through three mechanisms: it directs training effort towards specific weaknesses, it sustains motivation through visible progress milestones, and it enables systematic evaluation of whether training is producing the desired outcomes.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For SMART target questions, the most common error is failing to include both a number (measurable) and a deadline (time-bound). Check every letter. Edexcel uses “Achievable” for A — not “Accepted” or “Agreed.” For longer answer questions about goal setting and motivation, go beyond listing the five letters and explain why each criterion improves performance. A common mark-scheme trap: writing a goal that is either impossibly difficult or trivially easy — both fail the achievable criterion. Apply the goal to the specific sport or athlete described in the question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Goal setting directs effort, maintains motivation and enables evaluation of progress. Short-term goals provide stepping stones toward long-term goals and sustain motivation when the ultimate target feels distant.
  • The SMART framework: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-bound. All five criteria must be met for a goal to be truly effective. Edexcel uses “Achievable” for A, not “Accepted.”
  • Goals accepted by the performer generate greater intrinsic motivation than those imposed externally. Regularly reviewing and updating goals keeps them relevant and ensures they remain genuinely challenging.

lessons.title: Guidance and Feedback in Sport
lessons.description: Visual, verbal, manual and mechanical guidance and the four types of feedback used to improve performance.
lessons.content_html:
Guidance: How Coaches Communicate a Skill

Before a performer can improve, they need to understand what the skill looks like and how to produce it. Guidance is the process by which a coach communicates the nature of a skill to the learner. The four types of guidance — visual, verbal, manual and mechanical — differ in the channel through which the information is delivered, and each has specific advantages and disadvantages that make it more or less appropriate for different learners, skill types and stages of learning.

Visual Guidance

Visual guidance shows the performer what the correct movement looks like. A coach demonstrating a tennis backhand, a video of Adam Peaty’s breaststroke technique or a slow-motion replay of a gymnastic routine are all examples of visual guidance. Visual guidance is highly effective for beginners who do not yet have a clear mental image of the skill — seeing the movement creates a cognitive model for the performer to try to replicate. It is also effective for observational learners and for skills where timing and spatial awareness are critical.

However, visual guidance has limits. A demonstration by the coach or an elite performer may be too fast or too technically advanced for a beginner to process fully. If the demonstration is inaccurate, the learner will attempt to replicate the error. Video footage helps overcome the speed problem (slow motion replay) but requires technology that may not always be available. Cognitive overload can occur if too much visual information is presented at once — showing a beginner a full complex gymnastics routine before breaking it down can be counter-productive.

Verbal Guidance

Verbal guidance uses spoken language to describe or cue the skill. A coach saying “keep your elbow high on the follow-through” or “bend your knees as you receive the pass” is providing verbal guidance. Verbal guidance is quick, flexible and requires no equipment. It is especially valuable when a correction needs to be made mid-session, or when a specific part of a technique needs to be highlighted after a demonstration.

The main disadvantage of verbal guidance is that it relies entirely on the performer’s ability to translate spoken words into physical movement. For beginners, complex verbal instructions can overload working memory. The effectiveness of verbal guidance also depends on the coach’s clarity and the learner’s listening skills. Key phrases — cue words — are a refined form of verbal guidance that reduce cognitive load: “hips first,” “eyes on the target,” “tight core” distil a complex instruction into a single memorable trigger.

Manual Guidance

Manual guidance involves the coach physically guiding the performer through the correct movement. A gymnastics coach supporting a young child through a forward roll, a swimming teacher holding a beginner’s hips to help them feel horizontal body position, or a tennis coach physically moving a player’s arm through the correct backhand motion are all examples of manual guidance. Manual guidance is particularly useful for beginners learning dangerous movements (where the physical support prevents injury) and for helping a performer feel the kinaesthetic sensation of the correct technique.

The main disadvantage is that the performer may become dependent on the physical support and be unable to replicate the movement without it. There is also a safeguarding consideration — physical contact requires appropriate consent and must be handled carefully. Manual guidance is most effective when it is used to establish an initial feel for the movement and then progressively withdrawn as the performer begins to internalise the skill.

Key Fact

Four guidance types: Visual (see the skill; may overload beginners), Verbal (spoken cues; relies on translation to movement), Manual (physical contact; risk of dependency), Mechanical (apparatus support; removes fear but not natural movement). All four can be combined effectively and the appropriate choice depends on the learner’s stage, the skill’s demands and available resources.

Mechanical Guidance

Mechanical guidance uses equipment to physically support or constrain the learner’s movement. A swimming lane float that supports the legs, a trampoline harness that keeps a gymnast safe during aerial work or a batting tee that positions the ball for a beginner cricketer are all mechanical guidance. Like manual guidance, mechanical guidance helps the performer feel the correct movement and removes fear from dangerous or unfamiliar skills.

The disadvantage is that the supported movement is not always identical to the natural, unsupported movement. A swimmer who relies on a float is not using the same body position they will use in competition. Mechanical guidance is most effective as a stepping stone — it builds confidence and the initial motor pattern, but must be phased out as the performer progresses.

Feedback: Information After Performance

Feedback is information received about the quality of a performance. Without feedback, learning is slow or impossible — a performer who practises with errors repeatedly simply automates those errors. Edexcel identifies four types of feedback: intrinsic, extrinsic, concurrent and terminal.

Intrinsic feedback comes from the performer’s own sensory systems. A gymnast who feels that their landing was heavy and unbalanced, or a bowler who feels that the release of the ball was too early, is receiving intrinsic feedback. It is immediate and constant — available during every movement — but requires experience and developed kinaesthetic awareness to interpret accurately. Beginners often cannot distinguish between correct and incorrect “feel” because they have no established reference point.

Extrinsic feedback comes from an external source outside the performer. A coach calling “push through the hips” from the sideline, a video replay showing a fault in the golf swing, or the sound of the crowd’s reaction to a goal are all extrinsic feedback. Extrinsic feedback is particularly valuable for beginners who cannot yet accurately interpret their own intrinsic sensations, because the external source provides an objective reference point.

Concurrent and Terminal Feedback

Concurrent feedback is delivered during the execution of the skill. A coach walking alongside a swimmer calling “higher elbow, higher elbow” during a training length, or a dance teacher calling corrections as students move through a routine, is providing concurrent feedback. It is very immediate and can prevent errors from continuing, but it can also distract the performer or interfere with their focus during a complex skill.

Terminal feedback is delivered after the performance has finished. A coach who reviews video footage with an athlete after a training session, or who gives a critique at the end of a drill, is providing terminal feedback. It allows a more considered analysis and is less disruptive to the performance itself, but there is a delay between the movement and the information, which can make it harder for the performer to connect the feedback to what they did.

A very common error is to conflate these two dimensions of feedback. Intrinsic and extrinsic describe the SOURCE of feedback (from within the performer vs from outside). Concurrent and terminal describe the TIMING of feedback (during vs after performance). They are completely separate dimensions. Intrinsic feedback can only be concurrent (you feel something during a movement). Extrinsic feedback can be concurrent (coach shouts during a drill) or terminal (coach reviews with player after the match). Always explain which dimension you are using and avoid treating “intrinsic” as if it means the same as “concurrent.”

Beginners benefit most from visual guidance (demonstration), manual or mechanical guidance (physical support), extrinsic feedback (coach’s objective eye) and terminal feedback (considered review after practice). Advanced performers benefit more from verbal cue words (minimal interference), intrinsic feedback (tuning their own kinaesthetic sense) and concurrent feedback from a specialist coach. Matching the type to the learner’s stage is a core coaching principle — and a common focus of 6- and 9-mark exam questions in this unit.

Key Fact

Matching guidance and feedback to the learner’s stage: beginners need visual/manual guidance and extrinsic terminal feedback (objective reference they cannot generate themselves). Advanced performers rely more on verbal cues, intrinsic feedback and concurrent feedback from specialist coaches.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Edexcel’s primary feedback classification is Concurrent/Terminal (by TIMING) and Intrinsic/Extrinsic (by SOURCE) — not Knowledge of Results/Knowledge of Performance, which is a different taxonomy. Always name the type, define it in one sentence, and apply it to the sporting context in the question. A common error is to describe “positive” and “negative” feedback without explaining what they mean: positive feedback confirms what was correct (reinforcing the movement); negative feedback identifies what was wrong (corrective). For 4-mark Discuss questions about guidance, explore both an advantage AND a disadvantage of the type named in the question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Four guidance types: Visual (seeing the skill), Verbal (spoken cues), Manual (physical contact) and Mechanical (apparatus support). Each has advantages and disadvantages; selection depends on the learner’s stage, skill complexity and available resources.
  • Four feedback types by source and timing: Intrinsic (from within, during movement), Extrinsic (from outside, from coach/video), Concurrent (during performance) and Terminal (after performance). These are separate dimensions that can combine.
  • Beginners benefit from extrinsic, visual guidance and terminal feedback; advanced performers can use intrinsic, verbal and concurrent feedback effectively. Matching guidance/feedback type to learner stage is a key coaching principle.

lessons.title: Mental Preparation for Performance
lessons.description: Mental rehearsal, imagery and arousal control techniques that prepare athletes for competition.
lessons.content_html:
The Psychology of Preparation

Elite sport is won and lost in the mind as well as the body. A physically fit athlete who is mentally unprepared — distracted, under-aroused or paralysed by anxiety — will underperform against a technically inferior opponent who is perfectly prepared. The spec covers mental preparation strategies that athletes use to optimise their psychological state before and during competition: these include warm-up, mental rehearsal and the management of arousal.

The Physical Warm-Up as Mental Preparation

The physical warm-up is more than a physiological necessity. It also serves as a structured routine that transitions the athlete psychologically from a resting state into competitive readiness. A familiar warm-up routine cues the brain to prepare for performance, narrowing attentional focus, reducing distraction and helping the athlete reach the correct mental state. This is why elite athletes — from Dina Asher-Smith to Andy Murray — follow consistent pre-competition routines. The predictability of the routine is psychologically calming; it signals to the brain that this moment is no different from the many successful training sessions that preceded it.

Mental Rehearsal

Mental rehearsal is the deliberate mental practice of a performance. The athlete imagines performing the skill or executing the competition plan in precise detail, activating the same neural pathways as actual physical execution. Research in sport psychology consistently shows that mental rehearsal combined with physical practice produces better outcomes than physical practice alone, because it reinforces the motor programme, builds confidence and allows the athlete to mentally “experience” success before the competition.

Mental rehearsal is often used alongside imagery. Where mental rehearsal is the broader cognitive activity (practising a performance mentally), imagery specifically involves the richness of the sensory experience: the feel of the surface underfoot, the sound of the crowd, the weight of the javelin in the hand, the visual perspective as the ball approaches. Well-practised imagery is almost indistinguishable in the brain from actual experience, which is why it is such a powerful preparation tool.

There are two perspectives athletes use in imagery. Internal imagery (first-person: seeing through your own eyes as if performing) is most effective for skill execution and kinaesthetic feel. External imagery (third-person: watching yourself perform from the outside, like watching a video) is more effective for analysing technical errors or visualising positional and tactical aspects of performance. Many athletes combine both.

Key Fact

Mental rehearsal is the cognitive simulation of a performance or skill without physical execution. Imagery is a specific form of mental rehearsal that incorporates rich sensory detail (sights, sounds, feel, emotions). Together they reinforce motor programmes, build confidence and help athletes manage arousal before competition.

Arousal and Its Effects

Arousal is the level of mental and physical activation an athlete experiences. It is not the same as anxiety, though the two are related. Arousal describes a continuum from complete relaxation (e.g. deep sleep) through to extreme activation (e.g. panic). Every sport task has an optimal arousal level that produces the best performance. A dart thrower needs low-moderate arousal for fine motor control; a rugby player charging into a tackle needs high arousal for explosive power. The challenge of mental preparation is reaching the correct arousal level for the specific task — not too high, not too low.

Anxiety is the negative, uncontrolled end of the arousal spectrum. Somatic anxiety refers to the physical symptoms: racing heart, sweating, muscle tension, nausea. Cognitive anxiety refers to the mental symptoms: negative self-talk, inability to concentrate, catastrophic thinking. Both forms impair performance if they are not managed.

Techniques for Managing Arousal

Several techniques are used to raise or lower arousal levels to meet the demands of the task. To raise arousal (for under-aroused athletes in low-stimulation situations), coaches use energising music, pre-game team talks with vivid imagery, positive self-talk and physical activation warm-ups. To lower arousal (for over-aroused athletes experiencing anxiety), specific relaxation techniques are used.

Deep breathing (controlled breathing) is the simplest and most widely used arousal-reduction technique. By deliberately slowing the breath — typically inhaling for four counts and exhaling for six — the athlete activates the parasympathetic nervous system, counteracting the adrenaline-driven “fight or flight” response. A penalty-taker in football who pauses before their run-up, breathes deeply and exhales slowly is using controlled breathing to lower their arousal to an optimal level for precise motor execution.

Progressive muscle relaxation involves systematically tensing then releasing each major muscle group, starting from the feet and working upward. By experiencing the contrast between tension and relaxation, the athlete learns to recognise and release unwanted muscle tension. This directly addresses somatic anxiety — the physical tightness that impairs fluid movement.

Positive self-talk involves deliberately replacing negative internal dialogue (“I’m going to mess this up”) with constructive, affirming statements (“I have practised this hundreds of times and I am ready”). It counteracts cognitive anxiety by redirecting attentional focus from failure to process. A swimmer who replaces “what if I false-start” with “react to the gun, drive off the block” is using positive self-talk as an attentional control tool.

A pre-performance routine is a fixed sequence of physical and mental actions completed before executing a skill or competing. Golfers go through the same address routine before every shot; basketball players bounce the ball a set number of times before a free throw; gymnasts perform the same mental walkthrough before mounting the beam. The consistency of the routine serves several functions: it narrows attentional focus to task-relevant cues, it raises arousal to the optimal level for that specific skill, it triggers the mental state associated with successful past performances, and it reduces the impact of distracting environmental factors (crowd noise, opponent’s behaviour). On exam questions about mental preparation, mentioning the pre-performance routine and explaining its psychological mechanism (attentional control, arousal calibration) earns additional marks.

Students often assume that more arousal always means better performance — that a very excited, highly motivated athlete will always outperform a calm one. This is not the case. For tasks requiring fine motor control, decision-making under pressure or sustained technical precision (a golf putt, a snooker break, a gymnastic beam routine), excessive arousal causes tremor, loss of coordination and poor decision-making. The optimal arousal level for fine motor tasks is significantly lower than for gross motor tasks like a sprint start or a rugby tackle. Over-arousal is a genuine performance hazard. This is why mental preparation focuses on reaching the RIGHT level of arousal, not the highest level.

Key Fact

Arousal-reduction techniques: deep breathing (activates parasympathetic nervous system, slows heart rate), progressive muscle relaxation (releases somatic tension by systematically contracting then releasing muscle groups), positive self-talk (redirects attention from anxiety-generating thoughts to process cues). All three can be used in the minutes before competition.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about mental rehearsal, explain what it is (mentally simulating a performance in detail), why it works (reinforces motor programmes, builds confidence) and how it is used by an athlete (e.g. a high diver mentally performing their routine in detail before mounting the board). A common error is to describe mental rehearsal as simply “thinking about the sport” — that is not specific enough. For arousal questions, remember that the goal is optimal arousal, not maximum arousal. Name the technique, explain the mechanism (not just the outcome), and apply it to the specific sport in the question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mental rehearsal involves cognitively simulating a performance without physical execution; imagery adds rich sensory detail. Both reinforce motor programmes and build pre-competition confidence by allowing the athlete to mentally experience success.
  • Arousal is a continuum of activation from sleep to extreme excitement. Each sport task has an optimal arousal level — fine motor skills require lower arousal, gross motor tasks higher. Over-arousal causes anxiety and impairs performance.
  • Techniques for controlling arousal: deep breathing and progressive muscle relaxation lower arousal by activating the parasympathetic nervous system and releasing muscle tension. Positive self-talk and pre-performance routines help maintain attentional focus and reach the optimal mental state.

practice_questions.text: A club-level sprinter uses mental rehearsal as part of her pre-competition warm-up. Analyse how mental rehearsal can improve her performance at a county athletics meeting.
practice_questions.marks:

Secure: Mental rehearsal defined; at least two mechanisms explained; mostly applied to sprinting; generally accurate.

Developing: Mental rehearsal described; one or two mechanisms mentioned; limited analysis of how it specifically improves sprinting performance.

Emerging: Basic description of mental rehearsal with little analysis.

Acceptable content: reinforces the motor programme for the sprint start without physical fatigue; builds confidence by mentally experiencing a successful start and race; helps regulate arousal to the high level required for a sprint without tipping into over-arousal; narrows attentional focus to the start signal and drive phase; the sprinter arrives at the blocks having already “run” the race successfully in her mind, reducing the novelty and unpredictability of the competition environment.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which mental preparation strategies can improve sporting performance, considering evidence both for and against their effectiveness.

Mastering: Full evaluation of mental preparation strategies (mental rehearsal, imagery, arousal management, pre-performance routines); evidence of effectiveness discussed; limitations acknowledged (strategies require practice to be effective; novices may lack the kinaesthetic experience to make imagery meaningful; high anxiety may overwhelm technique-based strategies; other factors such as physical fitness and tactical knowledge also determine performance); consistent sporting examples; balanced, justified conclusion.

Secure: At least two strategies discussed with evidence of effectiveness; some limitations present; sporting examples used; conclusion reached.

Developing: Mainly benefits described; limited limitations; some sporting examples; argument largely one-sided.

Emerging: Basic description of mental preparation with little evaluative content.

For effectiveness: mental rehearsal + physical practice produces better outcomes than physical practice alone; arousal management enables performers to reach optimal states for specific tasks; pre-performance routines shown to stabilise performance under pressure; widely used by elite performers (consistent, structured routines before major events).

Against: strategies require long practice to work; novices may be unable to create meaningful imagery because they lack the kinaesthetic experience; no strategy eliminates the physical and tactical factors that also determine outcome; under extreme competition pressure, even well-practised routines can break down; not equally effective for all performers or all sports. Conclusion: mental preparation is an evidence-supported and important component of performance, particularly at elite level, but it is most effective as part of a comprehensive preparation that includes physical training, tactical knowledge and competition experience.
